Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

vignette:
Daniel, a 22-year-old Latin American man working as a product manager, had been in a city that was no longer behaving like a city should. He had gone there briefly with family visiting from the United States, and what had begun as an ordinary stay was shattered by the sudden violence of a war zone: sirens that never seemed to stop, the crack of gunfire in the distance, and people ducking into doorways whenever an unfamiliar sound passed through the street. One afternoon, while he was moving through a crowded market, a burst of chaos erupted nearby and everyone around him scattered at once. He did not see exactly where it came from, only the way bodies surged and then froze, the way a nearby movement could mean safety or death. In that moment Daniel became acutely aware of his own body as something exposed and unreliable, and even after he got away, his muscles stayed braced as if he were still waiting for impact. When he returned home, the ordinary world did not feel ordinary again. His body remained on alert, tense from morning to night, and he found himself scanning sidewalks, entrances, and the faces of strangers with a kind of watchfulness he could not switch off. Any unexpected movement near him-a coworker passing quickly behind his chair, a door slamming in his apartment building, someone stepping into his line of sight-made him react as though danger were seconds away.  

Over the following weeks, that persistent sense of threat began shaping what he did to get through the day. Daniel started checking his body constantly, pressing at his arms and ribs, looking for signs of injury or danger that might explain the tightness he felt inside. He kept asking his girlfriend, his sister, and even coworkers to reassure him that he was okay, that nothing was wrong with him, that he was safe in the office or on the train home. He said he knew the questions could sound excessive, but he could not shake the fear that if he stopped monitoring himself, he would miss something important and be caught off guard. When the tension became unbearable, he hurt himself physically to release the pressure, describing it not as wanting to die but as wanting a sharp, immediate relief from the feeling that his whole body was locked in alarm. For a little while after, the intensity dropped enough for him to breathe, and that temporary easing made the pattern hard to resist.  

Yet Daniel also noticed that these attempts to manage the fear did not really settle it. After each episode of reassurance seeking or self-harm, he became even more preoccupied with whether his body was damaged, unstable, or about to betray him again. The brief relief gave way to fresh fear, and he found himself back in the same cycle of scanning his skin, tensing at movement, and waiting for the next surge of panic. At work, in his role as a product manager, he began keeping his camera off in meetings and sitting where he could see the door, not because he wanted to be distant, but because he felt safer being ready to react. He grew more withdrawn with friends, partly because he was embarrassed by how often he needed reassurance and partly because he feared they would not understand why a normal office conversation or a sudden noise on the street could leave him braced and startled. Over time, the shame of needing to be soothed and the frustration of not being able to calm his own body made him rely on those habits even more, and the vigilance only sharpened.  

By the time he sought help, Daniel was exhausted by how little control he felt he had over his own reactions. He had come in because the constant tension was affecting his work and leaving him afraid that he was becoming less and less like himself. What frightened him most was that his body seemed to stay ready for danger even in places that should have been safe, and that every attempt to reassure or relieve himself only seemed to pull him back into the same alarm.
